From planned observations to a mixed model

Source: vignettes/repeated-observations.Rmd
repeated-observations.Rmd

A writer may complete several tasks on several occasions. Some scheduled texts may never arrive; others may be empty or too short for a requested measure. Keeping only successful scores loses the difference between these situations. Stacking several measures or overlapping windows as if they were independent texts creates a different problem: the number of measurement rows is not the number of observations.

This guide keeps the scheduled observations, submitted documents and calculated results as separate inputs. It then constructs a complete table and selects one declared specification for a conventional mixed model. The question in the example is whether a chosen lexical-diversity response varies with elapsed weeks and two named tasks, allowing writers to have different starting values and linear time slopes. The inputs are authored synthetic word sequences, not learner texts. Fitting them checks the connection between tables and a model; it supplies no evidence of development, proficiency or causation.

This guide requires the 0.3.0.9008 development sources or later. The helpers are installed example code, sourced explicitly below; they are not exported package functions. They use lexdiv_metrics_batch(..., plan = plan) and do not fit or choose a model. The table workflow needs no additional package. Only the model section uses optional lme4.

Start with the planned observations

The example schedules 18 writers for two tasks at weeks 0, 4 and 8: 108 planned observations. Its first observation is deliberately not submitted. Other authored cases include an empty string, punctuation only, three words, a document withheld from reporting and an unknown writer ID.

library(ldfreq)

demo <- new.env(parent = globalenv())
sys.source(system.file("examples", "repeated-study-demo.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE), demo)
record <- demo$record
helper <- demo$helper
print(head(record$planned, 6), row.names = FALSE)
#>  writer_id        task occasion observation_id scheduled_date
#>        001 description        0        obs-001     2026-01-05
#>        002 description        0        obs-002     2026-01-05
#>        003 description        0        obs-003     2026-01-05
#>        004 description        0        obs-004     2026-01-05
#>        005 description        0        obs-005     2026-01-05
#>       <NA> description        0        obs-006     2026-01-05
print(head(record$submissions, 5), row.names = FALSE)
#>  observation_id document_id input_characters
#>         obs-002     doc-002                0
#>         obs-003     doc-003                7
#>         obs-004     doc-004               16
#>         obs-005     doc-005              464
#>         obs-006     doc-006              456

Replace these two tables with your own scheduled rows and actual document map:

Input One row means Required columns
planned One scheduled observation Unique character observation_id, writer_id, task, occasion
submissions One selected document for a scheduled observation observation_id, unique character document_id, input_characters
results One submitted document and plan request Complete output of lexdiv_metrics_batch(..., plan = plan)
reporting One decision for a submitted document and request document_id, request_id, reporting_status, reporting_reason

Do not infer the schedule by taking every writer-by-task-by-occasion combination unless the design actually schedules them all. The example uses that design explicitly. Each observation can have zero or one selected document. If there are revisions or multiple attempts, declare distinct observation/attempt IDs or supply a documented selection or aggregation rule before constructing the map; the helper rejects duplicate mappings and does not average texts.

writer_id and task are character or factor labels, with NA for unknown values. IDs such as "007" remain strings. occasion retains the supplied type: elapsed weeks here, possibly a factor or date in another study. Additional atomic columns, such as the scheduled date, are retained. For CSV input, declare ID column types when reading; a leading zero already removed by import cannot be recovered. A submitted empty text has input_characters = 0; use NA if the original character count is unavailable. An unsubmitted observation has no row in submissions.

Keep the measurement and preprocessing identities

The example tokenizes saved English text with explicit NFC normalization, lowercase spelling and number exclusion. It preserves the full tokenization objects, original texts and the selected surface-token vectors. The plan asks for TTR and MATTR with a fixed ten-token window:

plan <- lexdiv_plan(presets = character(), specs = list(
  lexdiv_spec("ttr_v_over_n_v1", request_id = "ttr"),
  lexdiv_spec("mattr_sliding_step1_v1", list(window_length = 10),
    request_id = "mattr10")
))
stopifnot(identical(plan, record$plan))
record$condition

#> [1] "all tokens returned by lexdiv_tokenize_batch"
#> 
#> $resources
#> [1] "No external annotation model or lexical reference resource"
record$prepared[[1]]$provenance[c("tokenizer_id", "tokenizer_version",
  "normalization", "case", "keep_numbers", "input_characters", "output_tokens")]
#> $tokenizer_id

In your own analysis, calculate the complete batch with lexdiv_metrics_batch(tokens, plan = plan). For raw text, prepare tokens with lexdiv_tokenize_batch() first, as the installed example does. lexdiv_metrics_text_batch() does not accept plan in this workflow. For imported annotations, explicitly select the unit and inclusion policy and retain the original annotation/model/dictionary records beside the selected tokens; see Japanese annotations and annotated corpora.

condition_id labels the caller’s preprocessing and resource policy. The helper checks the metric plan, parameters, IDs and row coverage; the label alone cannot prove that every document used the same preprocessing. Save and inspect the actual tokenization, selections and resource identities. Different word units, inclusion policies or reference resources require separately declared conditions. A plan’s request_id and specification_id identify a measurement request and its computational specification, not a study design.

Build the complete study table 

study <- helper$study_long_table(
  record$planned, record$submissions, record$results, record$plan,
  condition_id = record$condition$id, reporting = record$reporting
)
stopifnot(identical(study, record$study))
view <- subset(study, request_id == "mattr10")
print(head(view[c("observation_id", "input_status", "N", "value")], 7),
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
#>  observation_id       input_status  N value
#>         obs-001      not_submitted NA    NA
#>         obs-002         empty_text  0    NA
#>         obs-003 no_selected_tokens  0    NA
#>         obs-004    selected_tokens  3    NA
#>         obs-005    selected_tokens 80 0.694
#>         obs-006    selected_tokens 80 0.655
#>         obs-007    selected_tokens 80 0.585
print(head(view[c("observation_id", "missing_reason", "reporting_status")], 7),
  row.names = FALSE)
#>  observation_id                    missing_reason reporting_status
#>         obs-001                              <NA>     not_screened
#>         obs-002                       empty_input           report
#>         obs-003                       empty_input           report
#>         obs-004 too_short_for_requested_parameter           report
#>         obs-005                              <NA>         withhold
#>         obs-006                              <NA>           report
#>         obs-007                              <NA>           report

The long table has 216 rows: 108 planned observations times two requests. It preserves the planned row order and then the plan’s request order, regardless of the order of submissions or results. Complete saved parameter and diagnostic list columns stay beside the scalar fields. The default allocation limit is one million rows; raise max_rows explicitly only for an intended larger table.

Keep the following states separate:

  • submission_status distinguishes submitted from not_submitted.
  • input_status distinguishes empty_text, no_selected_tokens, selected_tokens, unknown character count, and not_submitted.
  • computation_status copies the calculated ok/missing state or records not_submitted. The original status, missing_reason, N, V and value remain unchanged for submitted documents and missing for absent documents.
  • reporting_status is report, withhold, or not_screened. A supplied decision table must cover every submitted document/request pair and include a nonblank reason. Without it, all rows remain not_screened and none is selected for a model.

The empty string and punctuation-only string both yield empty_input from the metric core because both selected token vectors are empty. The study table retains their different source states. Three words yield TTR = 2/3 but are too short for MATTR10. The withheld document retains its computed value. Unknown metadata is not recoded as a new writer or task. Missing scores never become zeros. A report decision permits a computable score to be considered; it does not assert that a missing score exists or that measurement quality is adequate. The example applies no extra quality threshold: inspect below_quality_floor, diagnostics and your study’s reporting rules separately.

Select one response and explain the denominator 

selected <- helper$study_model_data(study,
  condition_id = record$condition$id, request_id = "mattr10",
  required = c("writer_id", "task", "occasion"))
stopifnot(identical(selected, record$selected))
print(head(selected$audit[c("observation_id", "not_submitted",
  "not_computable", "not_reportable")], 7),
  row.names = FALSE)
#>  observation_id not_submitted not_computable not_reportable
#>         obs-001          TRUE           TRUE           TRUE
#>         obs-002         FALSE           TRUE          FALSE
#>         obs-003         FALSE           TRUE          FALSE
#>         obs-004         FALSE           TRUE          FALSE
#>         obs-005         FALSE          FALSE           TRUE
#>         obs-006         FALSE          FALSE          FALSE
#>         obs-007         FALSE          FALSE          FALSE
print(head(selected$audit[c("observation_id", "missing_metadata", "included")], 7), row.names = FALSE)
#>  observation_id missing_metadata included
#>         obs-001                     FALSE
#>         obs-002                     FALSE
#>         obs-003                     FALSE
#>         obs-004                     FALSE
#>         obs-005                     FALSE
#>         obs-006        writer_id    FALSE
#>         obs-007                      TRUE
counts <- data.frame(Unit = c("Planned observations", "Submitted documents",
  "Known planned writers", "Computable MATTR10", "Model observations", "Model writers"),
  Count = c(nrow(record$planned), nrow(record$submissions),
    length(unique(na.omit(record$planned$writer_id))),
    sum(view$computation_status == "ok"), nrow(selected$data),
    length(unique(selected$data$writer_id))))
print(counts)
#>                    Unit Count
#> 1  Planned observations   108
#> 2   Submitted documents   107
#> 3 Known planned writers    18
#> 4    Computable MATTR10   104
#> 5    Model observations   102
#> 6         Model writers    18

The denominator is 108 planned observations, with 107 submitted documents, 104 computable MATTR10 values and 102 model observations from 18 known writers. One planned row has unknown writer identity, so 18 is the count of known writers, not a claim that the unknown ID belongs to one of them. Counts use a single response or the original rosters, not the 216 measurement rows.

The audit keeps separate flags for absent submissions, non-computable values, reporting decisions and missing required metadata. Flags can overlap and must not be summed as mutually exclusive exclusions. included is the final intersection. If the model needs an additional covariate, include its column in required. If every score is unavailable, the model data frame has zero rows while the complete table and exclusion audit remain available.

Selection requires one condition and request, one plan/specification/method, and one row per observation, with no reused document among selected rows. Do not pool TTR with MATTR, different window lengths, or overlapping window scores as independent observations. This table is for one selected document per observation; a window-level or multivariate model requires its own design.

Pass an ordinary data frame to lme4

The example treats occasion as continuous elapsed weeks and task as a fixed comparison of the two named tasks. Writers have random intercepts and time slopes. Writers and tasks are crossed in this schedule, but task is not a random sample of tasks in this model. A study sampling many tasks could need crossed writer/task random effects; tasks unique to writers are nested, and their identifiers must reflect that nesting. These are design decisions, not properties established by a successful join.

This illustrative formula assumes a common task effect and conditionally independent residuals after the writer effects. Within-writer task variation, shared visit effects, serial dependence or nonlinear change may require different terms for a real research question. Choose the time representation and covariance structure from that question and its sampling design.

Declare factor levels and contrasts before fitting, including after any table binding that may drop contrast attributes. The selected data frame uses observation IDs as row names so that the fitted model’s rows can be checked. na.action = na.fail prevents additional unrecorded row omission.

model_data <- selected$data
model_data$task <- factor(model_data$task, levels = c("description", "argument"))
contrasts(model_data$task) <- contr.treatment(levels(model_data$task), base = 1)
warnings <- messages <- character()
fit <- withCallingHandlers(
  lme4::lmer(record$model_formula, data = model_data,
    REML = TRUE, na.action = na.fail),
  warning = function(w) warnings <<- c(warnings, conditionMessage(w)),
  message = function(m) messages <<- c(messages, conditionMessage(m))
)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(model.frame(fit)), model_data$observation_id))
record$model <- list(
  fit = fit, formula = formula(fit), REML = TRUE,
  observation_ids = rownames(model.frame(fit)),
  factor_levels = levels(model_data$task),
  contrasts = contrasts(model_data$task),
  lme4_version = as.character(packageVersion("lme4")),
  diagnostics = list(warnings = warnings, messages = messages,
    optimizer_code = fit@optinfo$conv$opt,
    convergence_messages = fit@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages,
    singular = lme4::isSingular(fit, tol = 1e-4), singular_tolerance = 1e-4)
)
record$model$diagnostics
#> $warnings
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $messages
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $optimizer_code
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $convergence_messages
#> NULL
#> 
#> $singular
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $singular_tolerance
#> [1] 1e-04

If lme4 is unavailable, the table and saving examples still run; install it with install.packages("lme4") to run the model section. See the lmer reference for formula, data and missing-value handling, and singularity guidance for boundary fits. Preserve convergence and singularity diagnostics; do not delete random effects solely to remove a warning.

MATTR is bounded and its sampling behavior depends on the texts and window definition. A Gaussian linear mixed model here demonstrates data transfer, not a recommendation for every MATTR analysis. Examine residuals, the response distribution, variance structure and design before substantive inference. Keeping the scheduled roster makes missingness visible but does not establish an ignorable missingness mechanism or remove selection bias. The example therefore does not interpret its fitted coefficients as research findings.

Save the full record and replay the selection

Use CSV for a flat display; it cannot preserve parameter lists, diagnostics, factor levels, contrasts or all-missing column types. Save the complete RDS with the source texts, preparation records, plans, decisions and audit. Choose a persistent output folder for your own analysis; a temporary folder is used here so the example does not overwrite research files.

output_dir <- tempfile("repeated-study-")
dir.create(output_dir)
helper_path <- system.file("examples", "study-table.R",
  package = "ldfreq", mustWork = TRUE)
record$helper_md5 <- unname(tools::md5sum(helper_path))
record$helper_source <- readLines(helper_path, warn = FALSE)
record$session <- sessionInfo()
saveRDS(record, file.path(output_dir, "study.rds"))
write.csv(study[c("observation_id", "writer_id", "task", "occasion",
  "document_id", "condition_id", "request_id", "specification_id", "value",
  "N", "status", "missing_reason", "submission_status", "input_status",
  "computation_status", "reporting_status", "reporting_reason")],
  file.path(output_dir, "study-display.csv"), row.names = FALSE, na = "NA")
write.csv(selected$audit, file.path(output_dir, "model-row-audit.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE, na = "NA")

In a fresh R session, load the same package snapshot and set output_dir to the saved folder, then run the following. The recorded helper checksum checks the implementation used for joining; the full session record describes the package environment. Saved source is retained for inspection if versions differ.

saved <- readRDS(file.path(output_dir, "study.rds"))
helper <- new.env(parent = baseenv())
helper_path <- system.file("examples", "study-table.R", package = "ldfreq",
  mustWork = TRUE)
stopifnot(identical(unname(tools::md5sum(helper_path)), saved$helper_md5))
sys.source(helper_path, helper)
replayed <- helper$study_long_table(saved$planned, saved$submissions,
  saved$results, saved$plan, saved$condition$id, saved$reporting)
reselected <- do.call(helper$study_model_data,
  c(list(study = replayed), saved$selection))
stopifnot(identical(replayed, saved$study),
  identical(reselected, saved$selected),
  identical(levels(reselected$data$task), levels(saved$planned$task)),
  identical(contrasts(reselected$data$task), contrasts(saved$planned$task)))

This replay assembles saved scores without recomputing them or downloading resources. Recomputing scores is a separate check using the retained token vectors and plan. A fitted model additionally depends on its recorded formula, contrast settings, retained rows, lme4 version and numerical environment; its successful reload does not substitute for checking those conditions.
